title: Sentence and clause boundaries
summary: Recognise complete and dependent clauses, repair fragments and run-ons, and use agreement as one check that a clause contains a complete finite verb.

sections.title: Find the complete message
content: Compare “The volunteers checked every name” with “While the volunteers checked every name”. The first can stand alone; the second makes the reader wait for another idea.
Underline the subject once and the finite verb twice. Then ask whether the words express a complete message or begin with a word that makes the clause dependent.

sections.title: Test clauses before choosing punctuation
content: An independent clause has a subject, a finite verb and a complete message: “The bus arrived.” A dependent clause also has a subject and verb but begins with a signal such as because, although, while, if or when and cannot stand alone in this use.
A fragment is presented as a sentence even though it lacks a complete independent clause. Attach the fragment to the idea it explains, or supply the missing subject, verb or main clause.
A run-on joins independent clauses without a valid boundary. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but or so.
Agreement helps test the verb inside a clause. The head subject controls the finite verb: “The row of plants needs shade.” Full agreement and reference patterns are developed in E2.2.

sections.title: Repair meaning, not punctuation alone
content: Consider: “The rehearsal ended late, everyone missed the final bus.” Both sides are independent clauses, so the comma alone is too weak.

“The rehearsal ended late, so everyone missed the final bus” shows cause and result. “The rehearsal ended late; everyone missed the final bus” keeps the relationship less explicit. Both boundaries are grammatical, but the best edit also preserves the intended meaning.

Now consider: “Because the rehearsal ended late.” The opening signal makes the clause dependent. Removing because or adding a main clause repairs the fragment; changing only the final punctuation does not.

sections.title: Name the clauses before editing
content: For each item, mark every subject–verb pair and decide whether each clause is independent or dependent before selecting an answer.
Explain which boundary rule eliminates each wrong option.

sections.title: Repair unfamiliar sentences
content: Apply the clause test without prompts. Check sentence completeness first, then choose punctuation and conjunctions that preserve the intended relationship.
When more than one punctuation mark could be grammatical, use the wording of the options to identify the one complete and accurate revision.

sections.title: Diagnose the boundary error
content: Clause structure: I mistook a dependent clause or phrase for a complete sentence.
Boundary choice: I used a comma alone or separated words that belonged in one sentence.
Agreement control: I found the boundary but missed the finite verb form controlled by the head subject.
Option trap: I chose a revision that sounded smooth but changed the relationship or left another error. Record the closest cause before continuing.

sections.title: Control the complete sentence
content: Edit one unseen sentence that contains both an agreement error and a comma splice. A correct answer shows that you can locate the clauses, control the finite verb and choose a meaningful boundary.
An incorrect answer enters the retry queue after you record the closest error category.
